standard.title: Continuity and Change in Australian Life
standard.description: continuities and changes in perspectives, responses, beliefs and values that have influenced the Australian way of life
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined Cold War domestic effects, the long boom, and cultural transformation (K16); the Vietnam War's domestic effects and multiculturalism (K17); and First Nations and women's rights movements (K09–K12). They understand continuity-and-change as an analytical concept. They have not yet examined how Australians began to question traditional national values in the 1960s–70s as a connected pattern, or how specific governments shaped Australia's engagement with the Asia-Pacific.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain continuities and changes in perspectives, beliefs, and values that have influenced the Australian way of life — including challenges to traditional notions of Australian identity in the 1960s–70s, changing religious practice, and shifting approaches to Asia-Pacific engagement.

nodes.label: Traditional Australian values and their post-war character
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the traditional Australian values of egalitarianism, classlessness, democracy, and a 'fair go' as they were understood in the post-war period, and explain why these values seemed stable in the 1950s.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two traditional Australian values and explain why the long boom and Cold War consensus made them seem stable in the 1950s.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the traditional notions — egalitarianism, a 'fair go', classlessness, democracy — as cultural ideals (not necessarily realities) that shaped Australian self-understanding; examine how the long boom, social conservatism, and Cold War consensus reinforced these values in the 1950s; explain why the values needed to be stable before their questioning in the 1960s–70s is historically meaningful — change requires continuity as its baseline.
wider: Examine the gap between the ideal of egalitarianism and the reality of post-war Australia — analysing who was excluded from the 'fair go' (First Nations Australians, women in the workforce, non-British migrants) and what this reveals about the selective character of the ideal
Investigate how the Anzac legend functioned as a carrier of traditional Australian values — examining how it embedded egalitarianism, mateship, and stoicism as national virtues
nodes.hinge_reason: The 1960s–70s challenges to Australian values in N2 only make historical sense if students understand what those values were and why they seemed stable. Without the baseline, the challenges appear as abstract social change rather than as specific disruptions to a specific cultural consensus.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat Australian values as timeless rather than historically constructed. Making them explicit as post-war cultural ideals — with their exclusions visible — is the scaffold for understanding why they were challenged in the 1960s–70s and what was at stake in the challenges.

success_criteria: Describes at least two traditional Australian values as cultural ideals of the post-war period
Explains why the long boom and social conservatism reinforced these values in the 1950s
Identifies at least one group excluded from the ideal — showing that the values had selective application

nodes.label: Challenges to traditional values — Vietnam, feminism, and the Whitlam dismissal
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how Australians in the 1960s and 1970s began to question traditional notions, examining conscription and the Vietnam War, the Women's Liberation Movement, and the Whitlam dismissal as key challenges.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain how at least two of the three challenges — Vietnam/conscription, Women's Liberation, Whitlam dismissal — disrupted traditional values, and identify which values each challenged.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine how the Vietnam War and conscription challenged notions of duty to authority and imperial loyalty; examine how the Women's Liberation Movement challenged gender roles embedded in traditional Australian identity; examine the Whitlam dismissal (1975) as a crisis of democratic values — the Governor-General's use of reserve powers, the constitutional crisis, and the political polarisation it produced; explain how each challenge exposed the tension between the ideal of Australian values and the reality of power, authority, and exclusion.
wider: Examine the Whitlam government's reform agenda as an attempt to remake Australian identity — analysing how its policies on equal pay, Aboriginal land rights, no-fault divorce, and Asian engagement represented a deliberate challenge to the traditional post-war settlement

Investigate the 1975 constitutional crisis in depth — examining the competing interpretations of whether the dismissal was constitutionally proper or a subversion of democratic norms, and how this debate continues
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Whitlam dismissal as a contested constitutional event is one of the most analytically rich topics in Australian history — students encounter genuinely conflicting interpretations of the same events from people who were present. The Whitlam reform agenda also connects K18 to K09, K11, K12, demonstrating how the rights movements intersected with broader political change.

response_modes.reason: Students need to connect each challenge to a specific value being disrupted — not just describe the events. The scaffold is: what value did conscription challenge? (imperial loyalty, democratic choice over military service) what value did the Women's Liberation Movement challenge? (gendered division of labour embedded in egalitarianism) what value did the Whitlam dismissal challenge? (democratic accountability).

success_criteria: Explains how at least two of the three challenges disrupted specific traditional values
Connects each challenge to a specific value being questioned — not merely describes the event
Explains the Whitlam dismissal as a crisis of democratic values — what was contested and why

nodes.label: Changing religious landscape
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the changing nature of religion in Australia — including the declining practice of mainstream Christianity, the growth of non-Christian religions, and the emergence of non-traditional churches.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two changes in Australia's religious landscape since the post-war period and explain the causes of each.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the post-war dominance of mainstream Christian denominations in Australian public and private life; trace the decline in practice of mainstream Christianity from the 1960s; examine the growth of non-Christian religions through successive migration waves (Buddhism, Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism); examine the emergence of Pentecostal and non-traditional Christian churches; explain the causes of each change — secularisation, migration, generational change, the loss of institutional authority following abuse scandals; connect to the broader theme of changing values and beliefs.
wider: Examine the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (2013–17) as a major event in the declining authority of mainstream Christian institutions — analysing its findings and their effects on public attitudes to religion
Investigate how Australia's religious diversity compares with other comparable countries — examining whether Australia's trajectory of secularisation and diversification is typical or distinctive

response_modes.reason: Examining multiple threads in religious change — declining mainstream practice, migration-driven diversification, non-traditional church growth — gives a fuller and more accurate picture than focusing on secularisation alone. Each thread has its own causes and each contributes differently to the changing religious landscape.

success_criteria: Describes at least two changes in Australia's religious landscape since the post-war period
Explains the causes of each change identified
Connects religious change to the broader theme of changing values and beliefs

nodes.label: Asia-Pacific engagement — Keating versus Howard
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare the Asia-Pacific engagement policies of the Keating and Howard governments, evaluating how each reflected different approaches to Australian identity and values.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least one key feature of each government's approach to Asia-Pacific engagement and explain the values difference each approach reflects.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine Keating's (1991–1996) Asia-Pacific engagement agenda — APEC leadership, Redfern Speech, republican movement, engagement with Asia as Australia's economic and strategic destiny; examine Howard's (1996–2007) approach — stronger re-emphasis on US alliance and 'Anglosphere' ties, more cautious engagement with Asia, the Tampa affair and Pacific Solution as expressions of border sovereignty; evaluate how each approach reflected different understandings of Australian identity — Keating's post-British Asia-facing identity versus Howard's more traditional Anglo-American alignment.
wider: Examine how the Keating–Howard contrast played out in specific policy decisions — comparing their approaches to East Timor, the republic referendum, and APEC to evaluate which approach better served Australia's long-term interests

Investigate how Australia's relationship with China has evolved since the end of the Cold War — examining how economic integration and strategic competition have created a distinctive tension in Australian foreign policy
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Keating–Howard contrast is a genuine values debate that connects historical study directly to questions about Australian identity that remain live. The China relationship thread connects K18 to K19 and invites genuinely contested analytical argument.

response_modes.reason: Students need to understand the Keating–Howard contrast as a genuine values debate, not merely a left-right policy difference. Scaffolding the underlying identity question — what does it mean for Australia to be 'part of Asia' versus 'aligned with the Anglosphere'? — makes the policy comparison analytically meaningful.

success_criteria: Describes at least one key feature of each government's approach to Asia-Pacific engagement
Explains the values difference each approach reflects — not merely the policy difference
Evaluates how each approach understood Australian identity — with evidence
